note: Documented cases found by web search on 22 October 2026. Each claim is what the cited source reports. Where sources disagree, the case says so. A record may cite a case from this pool only; any other claim must be written as an inference from the model's principle.

cases.claim: A dissertation by Terence Wood at Victoria University of Wellington compares participatory budgeting in Porto Alegre and Belo Horizonte, drawing on 22 semi-structured interviews from April and May 2004. It reports real but uneven results, with obstacles that have held back what the budgets could deliver. It names two factors that shape outcomes: whether a budget can produce tangible results, and how much a city's population needs municipal services. The two cities' budgets produced some similar outcomes and some different ones.
cases.source: Terence Wood, dissertation 'Participatory Democracy in Porto Alegre and Belo Horizonte', Victoria University of Wellington (year not shown in the result); Portuguese-language article in the journal Ensaios (year not shown), for the 1989 start
cases.caveat: No quantitative impact study appeared in the results, and the evidence is 22 interviews. The 1989 start comes from the Ensaios article, which covers 1989 to 1995, not from the dissertation. A secondary summary with figures on water, roads and schools was not used, because its source page could not be identified in the results.

cases.case: Women as village-council heads in India's panchayats
cases.years: reservation since the mid-1990s; study published 2004
cases.claim: Since the mid-1990s, a random reservation of one third of village-council headships (pradhan seats) for women has been in place in India. Chattopadhyay and Duflo use it to test whether female leaders change policy. They report that reserved seats change which public goods are provided: female leaders put more into infrastructure tied to women's needs. The published study covers 265 councils in West Bengal and Rajasthan.
cases.source: Chattopadhyay and Duflo, Econometrica (2004), vol. 72, no. 5; NBER Working Paper 8615 (December 2001)
cases.caveat: The claims come from abstracts and summaries; the full text and its results tables were not read. The sample differs between versions: the NBER abstract gives 165 councils, the published study 265. The record should give the published figure and note the difference.

cases.claim: Under the 1980s contract system, regional governments struck separate deals with Beijing. The 1994 tax-assignment reform (fenshuizhi) moved revenue sharing at least partly toward fixed rules. Its results are disputed: a paper hosted by the Chinese University of Hong Kong calls early results mixed at best, while an IDEAS/RePEc working paper views the reform as having met its two ratio goals, for the central share of revenue and for revenue relative to GDP, and as having aided growth.
cases.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong paper on the 1994 reform (year not shown); IDEAS/RePEc working paper 0312 (year not shown)
cases.caveat: Both papers were read only through search summaries, and the results give no authors' names for them. The IDEAS paper is at https://ideas.repec.org/p/ays/ispwps/paper0312.html and takes the opposite view. Central revenue shares for 1984 and 1993 came from an unidentified web source and are not used. The record must name the authors after checking the papers.

cases.claim: Kerala's decentralised planning campaign had a 1996 target of 35 to 40 per cent for local bodies. A DMEO document (Decentralized Planning Experience in Kerala) reports that around 90 per cent of that commitment was devolved, and that the devolved money carried rules: productive sectors at least 30 per cent, infrastructure at most 30 per cent, and women's development at least 10 per cent. A table attributed to Oommen (2014), reproduced in an MPRA working paper, puts local plan grants at roughly a quarter of state plan outlay on average over 1997-98 to 2011-12. It peaks near 33 per cent in 2002-03 and falls to about 23 per cent by 2011-12.
cases.source: DMEO document 'Decentralized Planning Experience in Kerala' (year not shown); MPRA working paper 65710, reproducing a table by Oommen (2014)
cases.caveat: The DMEO excerpt does not say what the 90 per cent is a share of. Applied to the 35 to 40 per cent base it implies about 31 to 36 per cent of plan funds, while the Oommen table averages about a quarter, so the two sources conflict and the record must give both. Only search excerpts were read; the full DMEO text and the Oommen paper were not. Reader highlights and a publisher's blurb were not used.

cases.case: Fascist replacement of elected mayors by podestà, 1926
cases.claim: An Italian-language anthology dates the end of elected municipal government to 1926. It points to two so-called fascistissime laws and a royal decree of 3 September 1926, and it says that the appointed podestà, serving five-year terms, took over the powers of the mayor, the executive committee and the council. A study of podestà in Bolzano province by Andrea Di Michele dates the reform to two stages between February and September 1926 and treats the abolition of municipal self-rule as a precondition for the totalitarian state.
cases.source: Italian-language anthology on the podestà (2023); Andrea Di Michele, study of podestà in Bolzano province (secondary)
cases.caveat: Both sources are in Italian and were read only as search excerpts, not in full. The search did not confirm the legal instrument by name beyond the 1926 decree and the fascistissime laws, so a record should not name the instrument until an Italian legal source is checked. The link to the Di Michele study was not captured.

cases.case: Chile's 1981 transfer of public schools to municipalities
cases.claim: The 1981 reform put public schools under municipal control and funded them through a per-capita voucher, with identical amounts for public and private schools. A World Bank study by Donald Winkler and Taryn Rounds (1993), covering 1981 to 1990, finds mixed results. Whether the reform improved cost-effectiveness remains unresolved. Non-teaching posts at the education ministry shrank by more than half, and measured learning appears to have slipped. A slight cost-effectiveness edge went to private rather than public schools.
cases.source: World Bank study by Donald Winkler and Taryn Rounds (1993)
cases.caveat: The URL is the scanned text of the study, which the search summary says is garbled in places, so each figure must be checked against the original. The results give no clean causal estimate of the 1981 transfer on test scores. The 'more than half' figure is a summary's reading of that text.

cases.case: New municipalities in Chile and pupil results
cases.claim: An IDB study by Alcaíno and colleagues (2022) looks at 11 municipalities carved out in 1994 to 2004. Comparing them with areas whose secession bids fell short, it estimates a drop of 0.2 standard deviations in elementary maths in schools in the new municipalities. Staff churn and insecurity rose among teachers and school leaders there. Cutting the footprint of the original municipal networks, by contrast, made no difference to pupil results or staff.
cases.source: IDB study by Alcaíno and colleagues (2022), 'Government fragmentation and educational outcomes: evidence on the creation of municipalities in Chile'
cases.caveat: The search summary is the only source: the IDB record was not opened, so the 0.2 figure and the comparison design are as the summary reports them. The study concerns new municipalities from 1994 to 2004, not the 1981 school transfer, and measures elementary maths only.
